なに が すき です か — What do you like?
You say what you like and don’t like, what you’re good at, what you understand and what you have, and explain why with ～から.
Because I’m busy, I’m not going.
To say what you like: X が すき です (with が, not を!).
To say what you’re good at: X が じょうず / へた です.
To say what you understand and what you have: X が わかります / あります.
To ask “why?” (どうして) and answer with ～から.
To answer compliments modestly (いいえ、まだまだ です).
Yuki wants to start an international club at the university. She asks Mihai, Ana and Kenji what they like doing.
Let’s start a club! What do you all like?
I love singing. How about a karaoke club?
Liar! Mihai plays the guitar really well.
No, I’ve still got a lot to learn. Just a little.
I like sport. Football especially is my strong point.
Kenji, you’re also a very good cook.
Because it’s my job. But I’m bad at cakes. Because I don’t like sweet things.
And you, Mihai? You understand Japanese well.
I understand hiragana. But I don’t understand kanji at all.
Then how about a Japanese and Spanish club?
Good idea! But why not karaoke?
Because at karaoke we sing Japanese songs! It’s both.
I’ll play the guitar. But I’m not singing, let’s be clear!
I’ll cook. But I don’t have time on Wednesdays.
Then let’s make it Friday evenings!
the particle “ga” (with すき, じょうず, わかります)
I’ve still got a lot to learn (modest answer)
じょう = “joh”, one syllable with a long o: JOH-zu. Not “jo-u-zu” and not a short “jozu”.
A small っ = a short pause before the consonant: sak-kah. Like Italian “sacco”.
The u in す almost disappears: すき sounds like “ski”, だいすき sounds like “daiski”.
1. I like: X が すき です
In Japanese, すき isn’t a verb but a な adjective (“liked”). “I like music” is literally “As for me, music is liked”:
The classic mistake: “おんがく を すき です”. Wrong! すき, きらい, じょうず, へた, わかります and あります take が, not を.
きらい is quite strong. Japanese people often prefer the gentler version: あまり すき じゃ ありません.
2. Good at it or not: じょうず / へた / とくい
A politeness rule: じょうず is said about OTHERS, never about yourself (it would sound boastful). About yourself, say とくい (my strong point).
When someone says にほんご が じょうず です ね!, the Japanese answer is modest: いいえ、まだまだ です (No, I still have a lot to learn).
3. I understand and I have: わかります, あります
あります = “there is” (chapter 3), but also “I have”. “I have a car” = (with me) there is a car. For people and animals, “I have” is said with います: きょうだい が います (I have brothers and sisters).
How well you understand: よく わかります (well) — だいたい わかります (more or less) — すこし わかります (a little) — ぜんぜん わかりません (not at all).
から at the END of a clause = “because”. The reason comes FIRST, the consequence after — the reverse of English “I’m not going because I’m busy”!
Why aren’t you eating? …Because I don’t like it.
Don’t confuse them: から after a place/time word = “from” (くじ から); から after a whole clause = “because”.
おんがく を ききます (I listen to music)
おんがく が すき です (I like music)
にほんご を べんきょうします (I study Japanese)
にほんご が わかります (I understand Japanese)
ギター を ひきます (I play the guitar)
ギター が じょうず です (I play the guitar well)
Tip: if X is in a STATE for you (liked, understood, something you’re good at, something you have), use が. If you DO something to X, use を.
About yourself, politely: “Cooking is my strong point.”

クラブ の ポスター — The club poster
Yuki made a poster for the club and stuck it up next to the library reception.
Welcome to the Japanese and Spanish club!
Do you like Japanese culture? Do you like Spanish culture?
Don’t understand any Japanese? No problem!
Every Friday, from seven to nine in the evening.
Place: the second floor of the library.
If you like singing, if you play the guitar, if you’re good at cooking, come along, everyone!
No money needed. If you have time, be sure to come!
P.S. Tama and her kittens are here too.
What can you do if you don’t know any Japanese?
クラブ の はじめて の よる — The club’s first evening
Friday evening, seven o’clock. There are lots of people on the second floor of the library.
There are about twenty people. Yuki is very happy.
There are Spanish students, Japanese students and people from other countries.
Carlos loves anime. He understands a little Japanese.
Hanako came from Tokyo. She likes flamenco, but she isn’t good at it yet.
Sofia comes from Italy. Cooking is her strong point.
Sofia brought pizza. Both were very tasty.
“Kenji, you make onigiri really well!” “No, I’ve still got a lot to learn.”
Everyone laughed. Because Kenji is a professional cook!
From eight o’clock, it’s karaoke time.
Ana sang first. An old Japanese song.
Ana’s Japanese is still weak, but she sang very well.
Mihai played the guitar. Everyone clapped.
Then Yuki handed Mihai the microphone.
“Mihai, now it’s your turn to sing!”
“What?! No way! Because I can’t sing at all!”
“It’s fine. Sing a Romanian song, please.”
Mihai thought for a moment. Then he sang in a small voice.
It was his grandmother’s song. An old, quiet song from a village in Romania.
Nobody understood the words. But a deep silence fell over the room.
The song ended. For a moment, nobody said anything.
Mihai went red. “No, I’ve still got a lot to learn…”
At nine, the club finished. Tama was asleep under the desk.
“Come next week too!” said Yuki. Everyone answered “Yes!”.
